beats.beat: The company is a processor, not a mine owner or a bare trader: it takes minerals and processes them into additives and chemically modified minerals that give materials particular properties.
The DRHP groups its sales into four product buckets: Functional Additives (FA), Chemically Modified Minerals (CMM), Soft Minerals (SM) and Hard Minerals (HM).
It does not run the sales function entirely on its own: a long-term arrangement lets its corporate promoter, 20 Microns Limited, market and sell these products through its network.
Customer concentration is high enough to matter: the top 10 customers generated around 59%, 57% and 59% of revenue from operations in FY15, FY16 and FY17.
Exports are modest and concentrated: ₹10.68 crore in total over the past five years, to Nigeria, Saudi Arabia and Sri Lanka.

The filing's own list of strengths is diversified product portfolio, diversified user industries, import substitution, support of the holding company, product innovation and R&D, and a strong management team.

beats.beat: The DRHP restates six periods: the six months ended September 30, 2017, and the five fiscal years ended March 31, 2017, 2016, 2015, 2014 and 2013.

Profit after tax: the company lost ₹0.27 crore in FY13 and ₹0.12 crore in FY14, then earned ₹1.50 crore in FY15, ₹0.90 crore in FY16, ₹1.75 crore in FY17, and ₹1.33 crore in the six months to September 30, 2017.
Operating cash flow is lumpy: ₹2.01 crore in FY13, ₹1.28 crore in FY14, ₹4.22 crore in FY15, ₹8.03 crore in FY16, then a negative ₹3.50 crore in FY17; it was ₹1.25 crore in the first half of FY18.
Total assets stood at ₹30.19 crore at FY13, dipped to ₹25.93 crore at FY15, and rose to ₹34.25 crore by September 30, 2017.
Basic earnings per share: ₹(0.45) in FY13, ₹(0.20) in FY14, ₹2.47 in FY15, ₹1.46 in FY16, ₹2.43 in FY17, and ₹1.48 for the six months to September 30, 2017.

Contingent liabilities stood at ₹29.11 lakh as at September 30, 2017, and the filing notes that unsecured loans taken by the company, promoters or group companies can be recalled by lenders at any time.

Revenue from operations, EBITDA, debt and net worth line items are not in the extracted fact set; the writer must pull the full Restated P&L and Balance Sheet from pages 49 and 175 or explicitly say these are not available.

beats.beat: The promoter group is led by 20 Microns Limited — the same corporate promoter through whose network the company sells — and three individuals: Chandresh S. Parikh, Atil C. Parikh and Rajesh C. Parikh.
Pre-issue, the promoters hold 89,48,270 equity shares, or 99.76% of paid-up capital; the rest of the promoter group holds 21,510 shares, or 0.24%.
Issued, subscribed and paid-up capital as at September 30, 2017 was ₹897 lakh (89,70,000 shares of ₹10 each); authorised capital is ₹2,000 lakh.
Related-party transactions are structural: the DRHP discloses them for the last five financial years and the six months to September 30, 2017, and warns they may continue.

The company concedes operational and compliance gaps: it does not own the premises of two manufacturing facilities and its Bhuj and Udaipur administrative offices, and there have been past instances of late or incorrect filings with the RoC.
The extracted facts contain no particulars of litigation, auditor qualifications or regulatory penalties; that absence is a gap, not a clean bill of health.

beats.beat: Specialty chemicals are high-value, lower-volume chemicals sold for a particular function; this is the space the company operates in.

The Indian chemicals industry (excluding pharmaceuticals and fertilisers) was estimated at ₹5.8–6.2 lakh crore in FY17; specialty chemicals, excluding agrochemicals and dyestuff, were about 17% of that, or roughly ₹1 lakh crore.
Another DRHP estimate puts the specialty chemicals segment at ₹1,44,300 crore, and the segment is said to have grown at 10–12% CAGR from fiscal 2014 to 2017.

CRISIL Research forecasts specialty chemicals to grow at 12–14% CAGR; the DRHP also lists sub-segment forecasts of 10–15% CAGR for polymer additives, construction chemicals, water chemicals, personal care ingredients, textiles, surfactants and flavours & fragrances.
The market is highly fragmented — SMEs hold 70–75% share — and only a few Indian players have the scale or capability to compete with global giants on product development and innovation.

Import substitution is a stated tailwind: chemicals imports have grown at 6.4% CAGR versus 6% for exports, and China's stricter environmental rules have constrained its chemical manufacturing output, turning buyers elsewhere.
Policy context: a Draft National Chemical Policy aims to raise chemicals' share of GDP, FDI of up to 100% is allowed, four PCPIRs are approved, and GST came into effect on July 1, 2017.

Downstream demand that matters to this company: paints at ₹40,100 crore, organised cosmetics and toiletries at ₹43,000–46,000 crore, and polymer and plastic-product demand expected to grow at 9–10% and 11–13% CAGRs respectively.

beats.beat: 20 Microns Nano Minerals processes and sells specialty chemicals — functional additives, chemically modified minerals, and soft and hard minerals — used by industrial customers.
The company is tightly held: 20 Microns Limited and three individuals — Chandresh S. Parikh, Atil C. Parikh and Rajesh C. Parikh — together own 99.76% of the pre-issue equity.
It sells largely through its corporate promoter's network and, by its own admission, works on purchase orders rather than long-term customer contracts.
This is an SME IPO headed for NSE Emerge; the stated use of proceeds is a new manufacturing facility at GIDC Waghodia, Vadodara, plus general corporate purposes.
The restated numbers show profit in every year since FY15, but operating cash flow was negative ₹3.50 crore in FY17 despite a ₹1.75 crore profit.
The lead manager is Vivro Financial Services Private Limited and the registrar is Link Intime India Private Limited.

beats.beat: This is an SME IPO; the DRHP says the shares will be listed on the SME Platform of NSE, called NSE EMERGE.
The lead manager is Vivro Financial Services Private Limited and the registrar is Link Intime India Private Limited.

The stated objects of the issue are: fund capital expenditure for a new manufacturing facility at Plot 336, GIDC Waghodia, Vadodara, Gujarat; general corporate purposes; and creating a public trading market for the shares to enhance visibility and brand.

The extracted facts do not state the issue size, the fresh-issue versus offer-for-sale split, the price band, or the name of any selling shareholder; these must be reported as not disclosed rather than estimated.

offer.purpose: Describe the issue as far as the filing discloses it: listing platform, intermediaries, and the stated objects of the issue.

beats.beat: Sales run on purchase orders, not contracts: the filing says there are no long-term or definitive agreements with customers, and the top 10 customers bring in around 59% of revenue each year — so losing even one relationship is visible quickly.

Distribution depends on a related party: products are marketed and sold through the corporate promoter 20 Microns Limited's network, so a disruption to that arrangement hits the sales channel directly.

Some sites are on borrowed land and one plant is missing licences: the company does not own the premises of two manufacturing facilities and its administrative offices, and it has not yet obtained all statutory approvals for the Plot 9–10, GIDC Waghodia facility, leaving it open to penalties.

Cash flow can turn negative even in a profitable year: FY17 produced ₹1.75 crore of profit but ₹3.50 crore of negative operating cash flow, and the filing itself flags negative cash flows in previous years as a risk.

Related-party and promoter concentration are interlocked: related-party transactions have occurred over five years and may continue, and promoters control 99.76% pre-issue — minority investors are exposed to related-party pricing and governance choices.
